overview:
Samuel pours a vial of oil on Saul’s head, kisses him and names three signs: two men at Rachel’s tomb with news of the asses, three men bound for Beth-el who give him bread, and a band of prophets at the hill of God, among whom he will prophesy and be turned into another man. Then he must wait seven days at Gilgal. The signs come true, and people ask, “Is Saul also among the prophets?” Saul tells his uncle only about the asses. At Mizpeh the lot falls on Benjamin, then the family of Matri, then Saul, who has hidden among the baggage. The people shout, “God save the king,” and Samuel writes the manner of the kingdom in a book.

Saul is made king twice, in secret and in public, and both times he says nothing. He keeps the kingdom from his uncle, hides from the lot, and holds his peace when scoffers despise him (v. 27).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Samuel, with Gad and Nathan completing it (1 Chronicles 29:29); many scholars see it as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC from older sources.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it soon after the events (11th–10th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older court and prophetic sources.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The start of Saul’s reign, which many scholars place in the later 11th century BC; Acts 13:21 gives it forty years. Whiston’s margins to Josephus date the anointing to 1116 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Rachel’s tomb at Zelzah on Benjamin’s border; the plain (or oak) of Tabor; the hill of God with its Philistine garrison; Mizpeh, where the lot is cast; Saul’s home at Gibeah, often identified with Tell el-Ful north of Jerusalem.

hermeneutics:
Pouring oil on the head was how a great king installed a lesser one. In an Amarna letter of the 14th century BC (EA 51), Addu-nirari of Nuhasse in Syria reminds Pharaoh that when Thutmose III made his ancestor king, he “placed oil upon his head.” The letter recalls the act to claim Egypt’s protection: the overlord who anointed a vassal’s house was expected to stand behind it. Samuel’s words in v. 1 put the LORD in the overlord’s place. Saul is anointed captain over “his inheritance,” a ruler set over a people that belongs to someone else, and the title used for him is *nagid*, “captain” (9:16; 10:1), the appointee of a higher king.

The Hebrew of v. 1 is short: Samuel asks whether the LORD has not anointed Saul “captain over his inheritance.” The Septuagint is longer. Samuel says the LORD has anointed Saul ruler over his people Israel, that he will rule and save them from their enemies, and that this will be the sign that the LORD has anointed him ruler over his inheritance. The NET notes argue that a Hebrew copyist’s eye skipped from the first “the LORD hath anointed thee” to the second, dropping everything between, and the NRSV and ESV print the longer text. Read that way, the signs of vv. 2–7 are announced as proof of the anointing. Saul is not only told that he is chosen; he is given things to watch for that will prove it.

breakdown.label: Samuel anoints Saul captain over the LORD’s inheritance
Three signs foretold; wait seven days at Gilgal
Another heart; Saul prophesies; “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
Saul tells his uncle of the asses, not the kingdom
Mizpeh: you have rejected your God; present yourselves
Lot falls on Saul, found hiding; “God save the king”
The manner of the kingdom written and laid up
Saul home to Gibeah; men touched by God; scoffers

structure.summary: Two panels, a private anointing and a public choosing, each ending in Saul’s silence. Not a chiasm.

right.label: A′
right.text: The lot takes Saul in public

right.label: B′
right.text: The LORD reveals him; “none like him”

left.label: C
left.text: Silent to his uncle about the kingdom

notes: **King, delayed:** the word *melekh*, “king,” does not occur from 9:1 to 10:18. Samuel and the LORD say *nagid*, “captain.” It appears first when Samuel quotes the people’s demand (v. 19), and then in their shout (v. 24).
**Prophesying:** the verb *naba’* comes 5 times (vv. 5, 6, 10, 11, 13), and the two “signs” (vv. 7, 9) point to it.
**Taken:** the lot “takes” Benjamin, Matri and Saul (vv. 20–21), the same verb and procedure that found Achan (Joshua 7:14–18).

Chapter 10 completes the unit begun at 9:1: the asses lost in 9:3 are reported found (vv. 2, 16), and the private anointing becomes a public choice. Saul has still done nothing as king, and the scoffers’ question, “How shall this man save us?” (v. 27), is answered in chapter 11 (11:12).
**Forward:** the seven days at Gilgal (v. 8) return when Saul does not wait for Samuel (13:8). The proverb of vv. 11–12 is told again, in darker form, at Naioth (19:24).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 9, where God gives Saul another heart, is the Topical Guide entry *Man, New, Spiritually Reborn*. The entry sets the verse beside King Benjamin’s people, whose hearts were changed so that they had no more disposition to do evil, and beside Alma’s question to the church in Zarahemla, whether its members had “experienced this mighty change” in their hearts. The Topical Guide files Saul’s new heart under the same heading, and the rest of 1 Samuel shows that such a heart could be lost.

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The Church’s footnotes to v. 25 point to the Topical Guide entries “Scribe” and “Scriptures, Lost.” The second lists this verse with 2 Samuel 1:18 and the book of Jasher. Samuel wrote the manner of the kingdom in a book and laid it up before the LORD, and no such book survives.

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The Church’s Bible Dictionary entry “Anoint” lists v. 1 first among the passages where kings were anointed to their office by the prophets, followed by David (16:13) and Solomon (1 Kings 1:39). It adds that holy consecrated olive oil is used in the Church today for sacred anointings, including administering to the sick.

Josephus’s Samuel speaks plainly, “Be thou a King, by the ordination of God,” and names the Philistines as the enemy to be fought. He reverses the order of the first two signs and puts the band of prophets at Gabatha. Saul’s uncle becomes Abner, whom Saul loved above his other relatives, and Josephus explains the silence of v. 16: men envy those whom God raises up.

When the lot falls on him, Saul hides out of modesty, Josephus says, so no one would think he wanted the rule. After the people cry “God save the King,” Samuel writes down what would come to pass, reads it in the king’s hearing, and lays the book up in God’s tabernacle as a witness to later generations.

Pseudo-Philo leaves out the lot at Mizpeh altogether. As soon as Saul leaves Samuel, the people come asking for the king Samuel promised, and he tells them the king will come in three days; Saul arrives, and all the signs befall him. The writer then sends the reader to the book of the Kings for the rest, as if the details were already familiar.

The Aramaic translation turns the prophets of this chapter into scribes. Saul meets a band of scribes coming from the banquet hall with harps and drums (v. 5), and when a spirit of prophecy rests on him he sings praise among them (vv. 6, 10). The onlooker asks who their master is, and the proverb becomes “Is Saul also among the scribes?” The Targum also places the ark at Gibeah, the hill of v. 5, where the Philistine governors are.

On v. 12 Rashi reads “who is their father?” as a rebuke to the doubters: prophecy is not inherited, so why ask about Saul’s father? On v. 22 he explains that Saul hid among the baggage because he was running from high office, and he cites the Talmud’s saying that honor pursues the one who flees from it.

The midrash reads “the stuff” of v. 22 as the Urim and Thummim: Saul told the people he was unworthy and asked them to inquire by the Urim, hoping it would release him, and hid until they did. It sets him against Abimelech, who pursued rule and lost it (Judges 9), and beside Moses, who refused his calling for seven days at the bush. Whoever flees authority, it says, authority pursues.

The midrash takes Samuel’s cry in v. 24, “See ye him whom the LORD hath chosen,” as the first step in a pattern. Saul was chosen, then rejected when the LORD regretted making him king (15:11), and never brought near again (16:1). Aaron and David, by contrast, were chosen, fell under displeasure and were brought near again.

Augustine notes that every king consecrated with the sacred oil was called the Lord’s christ, beginning with Saul, “who first was anointed king” of Israel, whom David himself calls the Lord’s anointed. Yet there was one true Christ, whose figure all of them bore by their prophetic anointing. The very name Christ, he says elsewhere in the same book, comes from that anointing.
